dataset.what_one_row_represents: One caption line (captions.csv) or one topic segment in a 1-to-6-level nesting hierarchy (topics.csv)
dataset.time_range: Ali Wong's Baby Cobra (Netflix, 2016) — a single ~59-minute stand-up set
dataset.geographic_scope: Filmed at the Neptune Theatre, Seattle, September 2015

ana_01.label: Dataset profile: 925 captions, 131 topics, 59 minutes
ana_01.content: Baby Cobra is annotated at two resolutions. The captions table has 925 subtitle lines covering the full 3,535-second (58.9-minute) runtime; each line carries a laughter-duration value in seconds. The topics table has 131 segments arranged in a 1-to-6-level nesting hierarchy. Of the 925 lines, 352 (38.1%) triggered at least some laughter — the other 61.9% are pure setup. The loudest single line is at the 11:48 mark: 'Colonize the colonizer!' — which pulled 10 full seconds of laughter from the Seattle crowd.

ana_02.label: Laughter is 20.6% of runtime — below the headline benchmark
ana_02.content: Across the hour, audience laughter totals 727 seconds — 20.6% of the 3,535-second runtime, or 12.3 seconds of laughter per performing minute. Industry guides peg a headline-level comedian at ~18s per minute (about 30% of stage time spent laughing). By that benchmark Wong is running noticeably below, which at first looks like a contradiction to her reputation. The story will argue the benchmark is the wrong frame: raw laugh-time rewards joke density, not the architecture Wong is actually building.

ana_03.label: The hour is basically two macro-topics: marriage and pregnancy
ana_03.content: Baby Cobra looks like it covers a dozen subjects, but the topic tree collapses into only six level-1 segments, and two of them — marriage and pregnancy — eat almost the entire hour. Marriage runs from 6:55 to 37:35 (1,840 seconds, 30.7 minutes), and pregnancy runs from 37:57 to 57:17 (1,160 seconds, 19.3 minutes). Together they account for 85% of the runtime. The other four level-1 segments — intro, getting-older, a 10-second paintball aside, and the conclusion — take up 9.5 minutes combined. In structural terms, the special is a two-act play with a cold open and a coda.

ana_04.label: Laugh intensity by macro topic — 'getting older' is densest
ana_04.content: Measured as laugh-seconds per minute of stage time, the densest sustained macro-topic is 'getting older' at 13.9 laugh-seconds per minute (23.2% of the segment's runtime), followed by marriage at 13.2s/min (22.0%) and pregnancy at 10.9s/min (18.2%). The conclusion lands 11.3s/min. The 10-second paintball aside throws the average off — the audience laughs for 8.5 of its 10 seconds — because it is literally a one-shot callback bit dropped between the two macro acts. What the table shows is that each macro-topic maintains a very similar laugh-per-minute rate, which means the shape of the show is set by structure, not by any one bit being funnier than another.

data_table.description: Laughter intensity per macro topic (sorted by laugh-per-minute)

ana_05.label: Six levels of nesting — the routine has a file-system
ana_05.content: The 131 topic segments are not a flat set-list. They branch up to six levels deep: 10 at level 1, 21 at level 2, 43 at level 3, 31 at level 4, 19 at level 5, and 7 at the deepest level 6. The fact that the Pudding annotators needed six levels at all is the real finding — most club sets would bottom out at two. A level-6 segment is a digression inside a digression inside a digression inside a bit inside a sub-topic inside a macro-topic. That branching tree is what makes a callback possible: every bit has a parent to return to.

ana_06.label: Bit duration shrinks ~16x from outer to innermost level
ana_06.content: Segment duration shortens at a remarkably clean rate as you go deeper. Level-1 topics average 471 seconds (~8 minutes). Level-2 bits drop to an average of 156 seconds, level-3 to 82s, level-4 to 57s, level-5 to 47s, and the deepest level-6 bits are just 30 seconds long on average. A level-6 segment is ~16x shorter than a level-1 segment. The shape matches how narrative scenes fit inside acts inside plot lines — the show has a hierarchy that reads like a screenplay outline, not a joke list.

data_table.description: Average and median bit duration at each nesting level

ana_07.label: Laughter timeline across all 59 minutes
ana_07.content: Plotting laugh-seconds per minute across the whole runtime produces a jagged mountain range rather than a rising line. The audience is laughing from the second minute on — laughter never dries up. The densest clusters fall at 11:48 (21.75s), 8:00 (21.00s), 13:00 (20.50s), and 49:42 (the conception bit that closes the pregnancy act). Minute 20 is a trough (5.25s) — the audience is being set up. Minute 36 is the quietest laughter low of the full hour (3.75s) — a clear story beat, not a failing joke.

data_table.description: Laugh-seconds per minute across the full 59-minute special

ana_08.label: Two laugh peaks, not one: 12:05 and 49:42
ana_08.content: Running a 60-second rolling window over the laugh track produces two near-identical peaks. The biggest peak is at t=725s (12:05) with 27.5 seconds of laughter in a single minute — the 'colonize the colonizer' bit inside the marriage act. The second peak is at t=2982s (49:42) with 27.2 seconds — the conception fantasy that closes the pregnancy act, right next to the '...come with intention' callback. The two peaks are statistically tied; the 49:42 climax that the Pudding essay built its story around is the STRUCTURAL peak even if it is not literally the single loudest second. Readers who expect Wong's funniest laugh to come from her funniest sentence are looking in the wrong place.

ana_09.label: The three callbacks — gaps of 12, 33, and 46 minutes
ana_09.content: The entire hour contains exactly three explicit callbacks annotated by the Pudding team. All three land in the final nine minutes of the show, and each one reaches further back than the last: the 'hippies' callback at 49:43 reaches back to 16:35 (a 33-minute gap); the 'mom/third-world country' callback at 50:57 reaches all the way back to 4:46 (a 46-minute gap — nearly the entire show); the 'my pussy is wet again' callback at 56:48 reaches back to 44:24 (12 minutes). All three cluster in the pregnancy act, turning what looks like a free-standing third act into a retrieval engine that pulls forward from earlier threads.

ana_10.label: Callbacks out-laugh average minutes by 1.34x
ana_10.content: In the 30 seconds after each callback trigger, audience laughter totals 16.75s, 2.25s, and 6.0s — mean 8.33s. The baseline is a bootstrap of 1,000 random 30-second windows across the show: mean 6.23s. Callback moments out-laugh the baseline by about 1.34x. That effect is real but smaller than you would guess from a piece built around these three moments — because the callbacks' real payoff is that they chain INTO the conception bit at 50:11 ('That's right. 'Cause I don't wanna work anymore.'), which is the second-loudest line of the entire special. The callbacks do not land the biggest laugh directly; they set up the bit that does.

ana_11.label: What each callback actually calls back to
ana_11.content: The three callbacks pull from three completely different branches of the show. 'Hippies' (49:43) returns to a bit at 16:35 where Wong described herself and her husband as 'big hippies' who 'do ayahuasca ceremonies' — the payoff is her fantasy-conception line 'please look me in the eye and remember to come with intention, OK?' 'Mom / third-world country' (50:57) returns to 4:46 in the getting-older macro-topic, where Wong explained her hoarding by saying her mom was from a third-world country — the payoff is her mother's response to a miscarriage: 'Uh, yeah. Where I'm from, that's like losing a pair of shoes.' 'My pussy's all wet again' (56:48) returns to 44:24, where she had whispered 'my pussy is not as wet as it used to be' — the payoff flips the complaint into 'soldier glue... Neosporin' mucus at 7.5 months pregnant. Each callback lifts a specific phrase out of an earlier bit and lands it as the setup for a new punchline.

ana_12.label: The 10 loudest single lines — half live inside the conception bit
ana_12.content: Ranked by raw laugh-seconds, the loudest caption of the hour is the 'Colonize the colonizer!' line at 11:48 (10.0s), followed by 'That's right. 'Cause I don't wanna work anymore.' at 50:11 (9.5s) — the conception-act punchline — and then the one-off paintball callback at 37:45 (8.5s). Five of the top-10 individual laughs sit between 49:30 and 50:11 if you include surrounding lines, which is why the Pudding piece centered its analysis on that minute: a narrow 45-second window contains the second-loudest, third-loudest-ish, and supporting laughs of the whole show.

ana_13.label: Top 10 funniest bits — the conception bit is 38s laugh/min
ana_13.content: Ranked by total laugh-seconds per bit, the biggest wins are 'hooking up' (20.5s total, 35.1 laugh-s/min), 'bad drivers' (19.75s), '697-wet' (17.75s), and 'debt' (17.5s). But ranked by laugh density, the short '789-conception' bit runs at 38.1 laugh-seconds per minute — nearly a three-quarter laugh-to-talk ratio — in the 24 seconds right after the callbacks chain together. No other sustained bit comes close to that rate. The 'paintball' aside technically hits 51s/min, but it is a single-shot 10-second segment and is itself a callback, so the density figure is partly an artifact of scale.

data_table.description: Top 10 bits by total laughter, with duration and density

ana_14.label: Setup-to-punchline ratio: 1.63 : 1
ana_14.content: Out of 925 caption lines, 573 (61.9%) produced zero laughter — they are pure setup. Only 352 (38.1%) got any laugh at all. That is a ratio of roughly 1.6 setup lines per laughing line, which is considerably higher than the one-liner club comic's rate. Most of Wong's hour is not punchlines; it is architecture — the sentences that make the punchlines possible.

=== ana_14 ===

Implied setup-to-payoff ratio: 1.63 : 1

caveats.content: Laughter duration was annotated manually by four Pudding team members from the captioned Netflix file; values are in whole or half seconds and carry some subjective bias.
Callbacks are only the three explicit annotations marked by the annotators; implicit thematic return-visits are not labeled, so 'three callbacks' is a lower bound.
The paintball segment is marked as a level-1 topic but is only 10 seconds long — it functions as a callback aside between marriage and pregnancy and is not comparable to the larger acts.
